title: Startup Claims It Broke the Transformer Bottleneck—Independent Tests Back Some Boasts
summary: For nearly a decade, the transformer architecture has dominated large language models—and it has a math problem. Inside a transformer, a mechanism called dense attention compares every token (word or word piece) with every other token. For a 10,000-word text, that's nearly 50 million multiplications. Double the input length, and the compute cost quadruples—a quadratic expansion that makes LLMs notorious energy hogs. Subquadratic, a Miami-based startup, claims it has solved this bottleneck. Its model, SubQ, ditches dense attention for sparse attention: instead of multiplying all token pairs, it selects only the most relevant ones. 'If you're reading a book, you're not going to look at the first and second words, first and third—that's insane,' said CTO Alex Whedon. The result, the company says, is a model that processes up to 12 times more text at once than competitors, at a fraction of the cost, while matching top-tier coding performance. Initial skepticism was fierce. With only self-published benchmarks, many dismissed SubQ as vaporware. But now the firm has released results from Appen, an independent evaluator. 'That was really exciting to me, it validated their architecture,' said Jeanine Sinanan-Singh, Appen's director of generative AI research. The benchmarks confirmed substantial speed and efficiency gains on data-heavy tasks. Still, SubQ hasn't been released for public use, and some researchers remain cautious. 'Pretty much everything under the sun has been attempted,' noted Will Depue, an independent AI researcher and former OpenAI employee. 'It's not impossible, but it's akin to running a four-minute mile.' Subquadratic's founders are undeterred. 'We hope we're kicking off a new age of efficiency,' said CEO Justin Dangel. 'We don't think anybody will be building on transformers in a few years.' If SubQ delivers, it could reshape how LLMs are built—and slash the environmental footprint of AI.
why_it_matters: The AI tools you may use for homework or creative projects—like chatbots and writing assistants—consume enormous amounts of electricity. Improving efficiency could make these tools cheaper, faster, and less damaging to the environment, while also allowing longer, smarter conversations.

background_read: The transformer architecture was introduced by researchers at Google in 2017 and quickly became the foundation for powerful language models like OpenAI's GPT series (including ChatGPT) and Google's BERT. However, its self-attention mechanism requires the model to compare every word with every other word, so as the text gets longer, the computing cost grows quadratically—a major bottleneck for processing long documents or holding extended conversations. Many teams have tried to design more efficient alternatives, but most have failed to match the performance of dense transformers. Subquadratic, founded in Miami, entered this race with a sparse attention approach inspired by how humans skim text. The independent evaluator Appen, a company that provides data for AI training, ran its own benchmarks and found SubQ's speed and efficiency gains to be real, though the model still hasn't been released to the public. The cautious response from some AI researchers reflects the field's long history of transformer-killer claims that didn't pan out.

perspectives.description: For users and businesses, SubQ promises dramatically lower costs and faster processing, potentially making advanced AI accessible to schools and smaller companies that couldn't afford it before.
The model is not yet publicly available, and the AI community has seen many 'transformer killer' claims fail; SubQ may still stumble on tasks beyond coding or when scaled to truly massive sizes.

The quest for more efficient attention mechanisms reflects a broader trend in AI research: the initial breakthrough of transformers sparked a race to refine or replace them, with sparse attention just one of many paths explored.

If Subquadratic opens its model and it proves robust, the industry could shift away from dense transformers, prompting redesigns of AI hardware and software stacks—and maybe even reducing the carbon footprint of next-generation AI.
